records.title: New approach methodologies in nanomedicine: bridging the gap between in silico, in vitro, and in vivo systems.
records.abstract: The rise of nanomedicine has led to the regulatory approval of more than 80 nanoparticle (NP)-based therapeutics over the past two decades. Further advancement in the field requires a deeper understanding of the nano-bio interface of NPs, including their uptake, delivery, efficacy, toxicity, and adverse effects. Despite the heavy reliance on conventional cell cultures for NP screening, these models do not recapitulate the in vivo microenvironment, complexity, and physiological responses; hence, follow-up animal studies are required. Nonetheless, because of species-specific differences and ethical concerns around animal studies, developing alternative platforms has become critical. To address these issues, 3D cell culture models such as organoids, spheroids, and organ-on-chip systems have emerged to bridge the gap between in vitro and in vivo systems. Because they better represent cell interactions, gene expression, nutrient gradients, and tissue-specific functions, 3D models also align with the U.S. FDA's promotion of new approach methodologies (NAMs) to reduce animal testing. This review covers examples of organic and inorganic NPs tested in 3D models and discusses organ-specific NAMs, considering their advantages and limitations. The review also highlights how 3D models improve NP evaluation for drug delivery, toxicity, and targeted therapy, and provides a coherent NAMs toolbox for developing in silico methods for NP assessment. Future perspectives are introduced to underscore the importance of integrating in silico NAMs and 3D models to complement in vivo models for advancing precision medicine and improving the translational potential of complex drug products containing nanotechnology.

records.title: Animal Models of Slow-Transit Constipation: Current Progress, Limitations, and Future Perspectives.
records.abstract: Slow-transit constipation (STC) is a subtype of chronic constipation characterized by delayed colonic transit without obstructive defecation. Because in vivo human experimentation is constrained, animal models remain the primary tool for probing STC pathogenesis and testing therapies, yet no unified framework exists for judging howwell current models reproduce human disease. This review systematically appraises the reported STC animal models against a single validity framework and identifies design criteria for the next generation of models. We reviewed pharmacological agent-induced models (loperamide, diphenoxylate, alosetron, morphine, atropine), a physical stimulus model (ice-water gavage), surgical models (rectal distension, partial outlet obstruction, chemical ablation of the enteric plexus), and a naturally occurring inbred strain (the CFP/Yit mouse), and appraised each using the Face-Construct-Predictive validity framework. Existing models show substantial gaps in face validity (drug-withdrawal-dependent, self-limiting constipation rather than chronic progressive dysmotility), construct validity (few reproduce enteric glial cell loss, enteric neuronde generation, interstitial cell of Cajal depletion, and inflammatory infiltration), and predictive validity (induction agents confound therapeutic readouts). Advances in enteric glial biology, microbiota-short-chain fatty acid-motility signalling, single-cell transcriptomics of enteric glia, and genetic susceptibility point toward transgenic, pelvic-nerve-intervention, selective enteric glial ablation, and organoid-enteric nervous system co-culture designs, with sex-stratified evaluation and systematic clinical translation studies. The Face-Construct-Predictive framework exposes the translational shortfall of current STC animal models and defines concrete design criteria for clinically relevant successors, guiding model selection and prioritizing future research.

records.title: A review on MMP-2 modulating agents from natural and synthetic sources and their role in inflammatory bowel disease.
records.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is characterized by chronic intestinal inflammation, epithelial barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and aberrant extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), a zinc-dependent gelatinase, has emerged as a critical regulator of intestinal homeostasis owing to its dual role in tissue repair and inflammatory tissue destruction. Unlike several inducible matrix metalloproteinases, MMP-2 is constitutively expressed and tightly regulated through interactions with membrane-type MMPs, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), cytokines, redox signalling, and microbial factors. Dysregulated MMP-2 activity contributes to epithelial barrier disruption, leukocyte infiltration, chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and disease progression in IBD. This review summarizes the current understanding of MMP-2 biology, activation mechanisms, and immunopharmacological functions in intestinal inflammation, while critically evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at its modulation. Particular emphasis is placed on natural and synthetic MMP-2 modulators, including animal-derived peptides and endogenous inhibitors, plant-derived polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and rationally designed small-molecule and peptidomimetic inhibitors. Emerging nanocarrier-based and targeted delivery systems are also discussed as approaches to enhance selectivity and minimize systemic toxicity. Furthermore, the review highlights the limitations of broad-spectrum MMP inhibition and underscores the need for site-specific modulation that preserves physiological tissue remodeling while suppressing pathological activity. Advances in precision medicine, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, organoid-based disease models, and microbiome-informed therapeutic strategies are expected to facilitate the development of next-generation MMP-2-targeted interventions. Collectively, MMP-2 represents a promising yet complex therapeutic target whose successful modulation may improve long-term outcomes in IBD.

records.title: Repurposing antimalarial drug atovaquone in combination with radiation and PD-L1 checkpoint blockade to enhance antitumour response in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
records.abstract: Atovaquone is an approved antimalarial drug which could sensitise tumours to radiation and may modulate tumour immune microenvironment. Here we evaluated the triple combination of radiation with atovaquone plus anti-PD-L1 in HNSCC syngeneic mouse tumour models. We observed significant tumour growth delay induced by the triple combination treatment with differential responses in three different mouse models. There was complete tumour eradication in 6 of 12 mice in the MOCL1 model but not in the other two murine models. The triple combination was associated with increased populations of CD8+-T Granzyme B+ cells as well as decreased populations of Tregs, CD11b+Gr1+ granulocytic MDSCs and CD11b+ Ly.6G+ neutrophils. Atovaquone inhibited EGFR and its downstream signalling as well as reduced PD-L1 expression. The differential antitumour effects of the triple combination may be due to different basal and post-treatment levels of PD-L1, pERK1/2 and pS6, in particular, their levels were reduced by atovaquone +/- RT in MOCL1 models and not in the other two murine models. Radiotherapy plus atovaquone combination increased cell cycle arrest in G2/M phase, which led to inhibition of DNA damage repair by homologous recombination and increased cell death. We also observed increased activation of CD8+-T cells that led to enhanced killing in our HNSCC patient-derived organoid models treated with the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Overall, our results suggest that the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade has the potential to increase the efficacy of radiotherapy and/or immunotherapy. Thus, this may provide a rationale to further validate this triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in clinical trials to improve treatment outcomes.

records.title: Multi-omic profiling of 85 iPSC lines from familial dementia reveals cellular diversity and regulators of organoid development.
records.abstract: Systematic molecular characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines carrying disease-associated mutations is needed to distinguish disease-related biology from variation in cell state, genomic integrity, and genome-editing history, yet such systematic characterization is uncommon. Here, we profiled 85 human iPSC lines carrying MAPT mutations and isogenic controls using whole-genome sequencing, long-read sequencing of the MAPT locus, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation arrays. Single-cell analyses identified four reproducible iPSC states and candidate surface markers for their isolation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed unintended editing events and recurrent 20q11.21 duplications, which were associated with increased ID1 expression and impaired cortical organoid patterning. Transcriptomic analyses identified pathways associated with organoid quality and changes linked to clonal selection and editing, underscoring the need to use unconverted lines as isogenic controls. By providing an in-depth genomic characterization of MAPT iPSCs, this dataset serves as a proof of principle to enhance iPSC utility in biological research.

records.title: STING engages PKR to drive lysosomal cell death in lung ischemia-reperfusion injury.
records.abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) has been implicated in multiple forms of cell death. However, the effector kinases that couple STING to these death programs remain poorly defined. Here, we show that during lung ischemia-reperfusion injury, mitochondrial DNA release engages the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-STING pathway to trigger lysosomal cell death (LCD) in mouse and rat models. In human lung epithelial cells, STING oligomerization at the endoplasmic reticulum drives autophosphorylation of double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) at serine 33. This phosphorylation of PKR activates IκB kinase-NF-κB signaling independently of the canonical STING-TBK1 and PKR-eIF2α pathways. In turn, NF-κB induces LAMP3 transcription, promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and LCD. STING-PKR signaling is also observed in patient-derived lung epithelial cells and alveolar organoids. These findings identify PKR as a non-canonical STING effector and show that blockade of STING-PKR signaling attenuates epithelial LCD and lung injury.

records.title: Dynamic Graph Prior-Guided Latent Adaptation for Generalizable Single-Cell Perturbation Response Prediction.
records.abstract: Predicting transcriptional responses to drug perturbations in unseen cellular contexts is a central challenge in single-cell perturbation modeling. This challenge creates a need for models that combine flexible state transitions with structured biological prior knowledge. Existing data-driven models often struggle to generalize across unseen cell types, while many prior-based models rely on static biological graphs without explicitly conditioning prior influence on perturbation-specific target support. We propose DGP-LA, a dynamic graph-prior latent adaptation framework that refines biological priors and injects them as gated latent corrections within a cell-state-conditioned transition model. DGP-LA couples a transition backbone with perturbation-conditioned sparse graph refinement. It propagates gene-aligned target support over the refined graph and selectively injects the resulting topology-aware signal into the hidden representation. On Tahoe and NeurIPS, DGP-LA improves Pearson Delta relative to State by 8.7% and 35.8% for generalization across unseen cell types. In zero-shot drug perturbation response prediction on unseen cell types, it improves Pearson Delta relative to CRISP by 79.1% and 67.6%. The model also improves DE-gene recovery, response discrimination, and Hallmark pathway recovery, supporting adaptive latent integration of biological priors for more generalizable and biologically interpretable perturbation modeling. DGP-LA's source code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/bieyl/DGP-LA and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22155398. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

records.title: Benchmarking biological knowledge-graph priors against single-cell foundation models for Perturb-seq prediction.
records.abstract: Perturb-seq prediction increasingly relies on either biological graph priors or single-cell foundation models, but their relative value is difficult to interpret when architectures, split definitions and graph sources vary simultaneously. We benchmarked STRING functional associations and Gene Ontology co-annotation against dense, self-edge-only and exact-degree-rewired supports in one fixed graph-attention backbone, with a separate 200-HVG STRING-GO-control-co-expression sensitivity. Four public Perturb-seq datasets, three nested gene-space scales and three optimisation seeds were evaluated on held-out guide conditions; GEARS, scGPT and Geneformer were evaluated on the same held-out conditions, output-gene panels and Pearson-r metric after model-specific validity checks. At 200 highly variable genes, STRING-GO improved the equal-dataset Pearson r by +0.016 (95% interval [+0.010, +0.022]) relative to dense support. Dataset effects were positive in Adamson (+0.017), Norman (+0.015), Replogle K562 (+0.017) and Replogle RPE1 (+0.014), and 122/200 guide conditions improved (0.61 [0.54,0.68]). The top-20-gene Jaccard difference was +0.009 [+0.006,+0.012]. STRING-GO exceeded self-edge-only support by +0.024 [+0.018,+0.029] and the mean of ten exact-degree rewires by +0.011 [+0.005,+0.017]. The native-panel effect declined from +0.016 at 200 genes to +0.009 at 1000 genes; the 1000-200 interaction was -0.006 [-0.011,-0.002]. The primary graph-support comparison was formulated and conducted during peer-review revision rather than planned as an a priori confirmatory study. All three external models passed implementation-specific checks. Across 36 protocol-matched dataset-scale contrasts, 32 were within the descriptive ±0.030 reference envelope and four were outside, all favouring the external model. These results demonstrate a modest empirical predictive improvement under the evaluated matched protocol; they do not by themselves establish practical biological relevance.

records.title: AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing: from genome mining to the artificial intelligence virtual cell.
records.abstract: Fungi are important chassis organisms for sustainable biomanufacturing owing to their strong secretion capacity, metabolic diversity, and adaptability to industrial processes. Driven by the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), computational approaches that enable machines to learn patterns from data and make predictions, together with omics technologies and synthetic biology, data- and model-driven strategies are increasingly reshaping fungal cell factory design and optimization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing, covering AI-assisted genome mining, enzyme and pathway analysis, genome editing, metabolic network modeling, and intelligent fermentation control. The review further highlights the emerging concept of the artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC), which integrates multi-omics data, mechanistic modeling, and machine learning-based approaches into a unified multiscale framework for simulating dynamic cellular behaviors. The technical foundations and potential applications of AIVC in fungal metabolic engineering, drug discovery, agriculture, and environmental biotechnology are reviewed. Finally, key challenges-data quality and standardization, cross-scale model integration and interpretability, and the gap between in silico prediction and experimental validation-are highlighted. This review provides a systematic perspective on the role of AI and virtual cell technologies in advancing next generation fungal biotechnology.

records.title: PHAROS: turning single-cell perturbation models into target-directed drug-combination screens.
records.abstract: Combination therapies are central to cancer treatment, but exhaustive screening is impractical. We introduce PHAROS, a framework that turns a pretrained single-cell perturbation model into a target-directed search engine for drug combinations. PHAROS predicts how a cell population changes under a drug, one drug at a time, then chains these predictions together to simulate drug combinations. It scores each simulated outcome against the desired target state and uses a search algorithm to find the most promising combinations, all without retraining the underlying model. Across two independent combinatorial perturbation datasets, PHAROS recovered exact or mechanism-matched two-drug responses in cell lines, both seen and unseen during model training. Its rankings were specific to the requested conversion and were not explained by single-drug effects, additive effects, or shared mechanism of action. In exploratory analyses of patient-derived metastatic HR+/HER2- breast tumors and basal cell carcinoma (BCC), PHAROS prioritized FDA-approved regimens, distinguished combinations by their predicted tumor-versus-immune objective profiles, and nominated pathway-level hypotheses, while explicitly identifying both tumor cohorts as outside the model's supported distribution. PHAROS provides a modular route from pretrained virtual-cell models to inverse, single-cell combination-screening platforms.

records.title: Pop-Corn: Predicting Perturbation Phenotype Effects Across Single-Cell and Spatial Contexts.
records.abstract: Genetic perturbations can reshape cell populations by altering the relative abundance of specific cell types and states within the profiled population, including increases, decreases and states that become detectable after perturbation. Pooled single-cell screens, such as Perturb-seq, measure such responses at scale. However, only a small fraction of possible perturbations can be tested experimentally. A central challenge is therefore to predict compositional shifts induced by unseen perturbations. Many perturbation-prediction methods do not directly optimize for this outcome; instead, they predict gene-expression responses and infer cell-type and cell-state composition downstream. Surprisingly, we find that even models that accurately predict perturbation-induced changes in average gene expression perform poorly at forecasting these compositional shifts. To address this gap, we present Pop-Corn, a method that directly predicts how a perturbation reshapes cell-type composition without reconstructing gene expression. In the primary T-cell benchmark, Pop-Corn predicted the overall cell-state composition of held-out perturbations more accurately than the evaluated expression-prediction pipelines, while better preserving the diversity of observed cell states. We further extend Pop-Corn to intact tissue, where it predicts perturbation-induced cell-type proportion changes in local cellular neighborhoods and uses attention patterns to generate hypotheses about context-dependent cellular interactions. Retrospective virtual screens support the use of Pop-Corn to prioritize perturbations for experimental follow-up according to their predicted effects on cell-state composition.

records.title: Multi-Objective Molecular Generation via Actor-Critic Regulated by Adaptive Cooperative Evolution.
records.abstract: Many complex diseases involve intricate and interdependent biological mechanisms, making multi-target drug design therapeutically important. However, existing molecular generation models often struggle to balance conflicting property requirements, maintain structural exploration, and avoid premature convergence during reinforcement learning. To address these challenges, we propose CMIR-RL, a reinforcement learning-based molecular generation model that integrates cooperative crossover-mutation exploration, structure-based intrinsic rewards, and Pareto-based multi-objective optimization. In CMIR-RL, mutation and crossover networks synergistically guide the agent to balance exploration and exploitation, while Pareto-front-guided reward assignment updates the generation policy under multiple property constraints. Experiments on a three-objective polypharmacology task show that CMIR-RL significantly improves desirability from 0.8868 to 0.9542 over the baseline method, while maintaining competitive validity, uniqueness, and diversity. Additional GuacaMol results further indicate competitive generalization across goal-directed molecular generation tasks. These results show that CMIR-RL is an effective reinforcement learning strategy for early-stage multi-objective molecular design.

records.title: Virus-like particle vaccines: from antigen architecture to antigen presentation and adaptive immune responses.
records.abstract: Virus-like particles (VLPs) mimic key structural features of native viruses while lacking a replication-competent viral genome, combining favorable safety with multivalent antigen presentation and strong immunogenicity. Yet, how VLP design influences the quality and persistence of adaptive immunity remains incompletely understood. This review examines relevant literature identified through targeted searches on recent advances in VLP engineering, with emphasis on particle architecture, antigen-display strategies, and structural determinants of immune recognition. We discuss how VLPs facilitate antigen presentation by antigen-presenting cells and shape CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell responses, immune memory, and T follicular helper cell-B-cell interactions within germinal centers. Emerging approaches linking VLP design with humoral and cellular immunity are also considered. The next generation of VLP vaccines will require a transition from empirical enhancement of immunogenicity toward precision engineering of immune responses. A major challenge is to establish robust and transferable structure-immunity relationships while addressing manufacturing feasibility, quality control, potency assessment, and product comparability. Advances in computational protein design, structural biology, and high-dimensional immune profiling are expected to enable increasingly quantitative and mechanism-based optimization of VLP platforms. However, fully predictive control over human immune responses will remain a complex challenge.

records.title: MolecureAI: an agentic AI platform for autonomous drug discovery.
records.abstract: Accelerating the identification of viable drug candidates across therapeutic areas demands autonomous systems for molecular generation that enforce chemical correctness by structural invariants rather than model capability. We present MolecureAI, an autonomous AI agent architecture for closed-loop drug discovery with cost-ordered cascade evaluation that addresses four capability gaps unresolved across the field: autonomous design strategy selection, persistent cross-campaign structural memory, in-loop ADMET safety gating, and literature-scale evidence integration into the generative loop. A cost-ordered cascade concentrates full structure-based evaluation on a small pre-filtered survivor set, achieving a 2.5 × reduction in candidates advanced relative to those generated. An in-loop metabolic gate enforces Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) safety by writing flagged reactive substructures to a per-target learned state, suppressing identified liabilities from all subsequent generation rounds. A persistent campaign memory influences generation trajectories by embedding prior structural success and failure patterns directly into the design context. We validate these architectural invariants across three structurally diverse benchmark targets (EGFR, KRAS G 12 C , and BRD4) through a five-condition component ablation and a controlled memory ablation, and confirm generator agnosticism across four language-model backends via a deterministic recalibration layer that overrides backend self-evaluation bias. Without explicit chemotype instruction, the pipeline computationally converged toward candidates bearing the 4-anilinoquinazoline scaffold characteristic of the approved inhibitors erlotinib and gefitinib, from structural feedback alone. Persistent campaign memory showed directional but non-significant trends toward lower inter-round score variance and higher late-stage advance rate ( n ≈ 90 per condition; all p > 0.20 ). The component ablation reveals that optimizing for a single objective collapses performance on others; only full orchestration resolves this tension. Advancement rates above 79% across all backends confirm that the validated properties are generator-agnostic, enforced by architectural invariants rather than model capability. All reported outcomes are properties of the computational generation process; prospective biochemical validation of the advanced candidates remains the primary direction for future work.

records.title: Functional alignment of protein language models via reinforcement learning.
records.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) enable generative design of novel protein sequences but remain fundamentally misaligned with protein engineering goals, as they lack explicit understanding of function and often fail to improve properties beyond those found in nature. We introduce Reinforcement Learning from eXperimental Feedback (RLXF), a general framework that aligns protein language models with experimentally measured functional objectives, drawing inspiration from the methods used to align large language models like ChatGPT. Applied across five diverse protein families, RLXF improves generation of high-functioning variants beyond pre-trained baselines. We demonstrate this with CreiLOV, an oxygen-independent fluorescent protein, where RLXF-aligned models generate sequences with significantly enhanced fluorescence, including the most fluorescent CreiLOV variants reported to date. Our results indicate that RLXF-aligned models effectively integrate the evolutionary knowledge encoded in pre-trained pLMs with experimental observations, improving the success rate of generated sequences and enabling the discovery of synergistic mutation combinations that are difficult to identify through zero-shot or evolutionary approaches. RLXF provides a scalable and accessible approach to steer generative models toward desired biochemical properties, enabling function-driven protein design beyond the limits of natural evolution.

records.title: Perspectives on tissue-selective insulin derivatives.
records.abstract: Insulin is a central regulator of metabolic homoeostasis with diverse, tissue-specific actions across multiple organs. Despite major advances in insulin formulations, current therapies rely on systemic delivery and do not reproduce the physiological distribution of endogenous insulin, resulting in non-physiological tissue exposure and associated metabolic limitations. In this perspective, we discuss emerging strategies aimed at achieving tissue-selective insulin action, including molecular engineering of insulin analogues, modulation of insulin receptor isoform specificity and targeted delivery approaches. Attention is given to hepato-preferential, muscle-directed, brain-targeted and adipose-modulating strategies, highlighting their mechanistic basis, therapeutic potential and inherent limitations. While proof of principle has been established for several approaches, challenges remain in balancing tissue selectivity with whole-body metabolic control. Advances in protein design and delivery technologies may ultimately enable the development of next-generation insulin therapies that better mimic physiological insulin action and improve clinical outcomes in metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases.

records.title: Coordinating structure-guided design and cis-regulatory optimization to engineer elite herbicide-tolerance alleles in crops.
records.abstract: Genome editing facilitates the rapid creation of elite alleles, yet identifying editable sites for durable trait improvement without functional trade-offs remains challenging. Most current strategies modify a single genetic axis, limiting their effectiveness and stability. Here we developed a dual-layer allele engineering framework integrating structure-guided protein design with precise cis-regulatory tuning to overcome such constraints. Using rice 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (OsHPPD) as a model, structural analysis enabled the rational design of coding variants that retain enzymatic activity while conferring herbicide resistance. To further enhance resistance, we introduced a highly efficient 22-bp expression-modulating element into the engineered alleles, generating combinatorial coding and regulatory variants with significantly improved resistance, up to four times the recommended field application rate. Importantly, the dual-layer strategy was successfully applied in polyploid wheat, demonstrating its robustness and cross-species applicability. Our work establishes a versatile framework for functional allele engineering, offering a precise and broadly applicable route for crop improvement.

records.title: Advancing colorectal cancer management through clinical proteomics: from genotype to proteotype toward clinical translation.
records.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide, with outcomes depending on the stages at diagnosis. Genomic and transcriptomic classifications are largely inferential because the genotype-phenotype relationship is non-linear and is influenced by post-translational regulation, protein turnover, and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Proteomics measures this functional layer directly. This review surveys proteomic technologies for CRC emphasizing mass spectrometry, affinity- and aptamer- based multiplex platforms, post-translational modification proteomics, spatial proteomics, AI-driven structural and predictive analysis, and multi-omics integration. Each platform is evaluated based on clinical questions, the supporting evidence and the barriers to implementation. Literature was drawn primarily from PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus (2020-2026), emphasizing advanced and translational applications. Alongside approved blood cfDNA and stool-RNA molecular tests, proteomics is a functional complementary technology that may improve biological interpretation, assay triage and treatment response prediction, although prospective clinical utility remains to be established. The decisive barriers are standardized biospecimens, validation evidence, clinical utility data and interoperable public data sharing. (169 words).

records.title: Mitochondrial Quality Control in Degenerative Musculoskeletal Diseases: Signaling Networks and Therapeutic Landscapes.
records.abstract: Degenerative musculoskeletal disorders, including osteoarthritis (OA), intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), and osteoporosis (OP), are increasingly viewed as disorders of mitochondrial quality control (MQC) rather than passive mechanical wear. The MQC network, comprising mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy-biogenesis coupling, and inter-organelle communication, organizes the aging-inflammation-metabolism axis. Its collapse releases mtDNA fragments that act as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) activating innate immunity via cGAS-STING, and metabolic intermediates that remodel the epigenome through histone lactylation, potentially locking acute stress into a "metabolic memory", although the mtDNA-methylation component remains hypothesis-level. Multi-omics and cell-free mtDNA liquid biopsy underpin a proposed subtyping into bioenergetic failure, immuno-inflammatory activation, and senescent cell accumulation, still a within-OA hypothesis pending independent and cross-disease validation. Therapy is shifting from symptom management toward organelle medicine, including cardiolipin stabilizers, PROTAC-mediated protein degradation, mitochondrial base editing, and engineered mitochondrial transplantation. Metformin has randomized trial evidence in knee OA pending confirmation, NAD+ precursors are in early clinical testing, and SS-31 holds accelerated approval only for Barth syndrome; other strategies remain preclinical. Delivery barriers and disease heterogeneity require precision stratification, biomimetic models, and AI-driven decision-making. This review delineates the shared molecular logic of the three diseases and proposes a prototype subtyping-to-treatment roadmap pending validation.

records.title: Mitotic and meiotic midbody remnants: Divergent architectures with distinct clinical applications.
records.abstract: Midbody remnants (MBRs), once considered inert cytokinetic debris, are now recognized as architecturally specialized, translationally active organelles whose functions reflect the mode of cell division. This review compares MBR biology in symmetric somatic mitosis and asymmetric oocyte meiosis. In somatic cells, MBRs can be retained or secreted as large extracellular vesicles that carry midbody proteins, RNAs, and translation machinery; their enrichment in stem and cancer cells implicates them in cell-state regulation and identifies them as promising, though unvalidated, substrates for liquid-biopsy biomarkers and therapeutic targeting. In oocytes, meiotic midbodies form a distinctive ring-cap architecture that concentrates local translation and restricts maternal products to the egg, thereby supporting developmental competence. Together, these studies establish division mode as a key determinant of midbody architecture, cargo, fate, and translational potential, linking cytokinesis to cancer biology and reproductive medicine.

records.title: Treatment of Advanced Biliary Tract Cancer: ASCO Living Guideline, Version 2026.1.0.
records.abstract: This living guideline provides recommendations for liquid biopsy and treatment of patients with advanced biliary tract cancer. The American Society of Clinical Oncology convened an Expert Panel to conduct a systematic review of relevant studies and develop recommendations for liquid biopsy and systemic therapy for patients with advanced biliary tract cancer. Six studies provided estimates of concordance between liquid biopsy and tissue biopsy. Nine RCTs were included in the evidence base for first-line therapy. One phase III RCT and four phase II RCTs were included in the evidence for second-line chemotherapy. Eleven single studies or reviews supported biomarker-specific second-line therapy recommendations. Testing with broad-based tissue DNA and RNA NGS testing to determine the presence of targetable biomarkers is recommended at the time of diagnosis at any stage. Liquid biopsy with plasma is generally recommended only when tissue biopsy is unavailable. As first-line therapy for patients with pMMR/MSS advanced BTC, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) plus chemotherapy is recommended. Options for patients with advanced BTC who are not candidates for ICIs are included in the guideline. Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an option for patients with dMMR/MSI-H advanced BTC. For patients with disease progression on first-line treatment and who have no identified biomarkers, FOLFOX with active symptom control, or active symptom control alone are recommended; options for patients who are ineligible for oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy are included in the guideline. Second-line therapy options are recommended for patients with dMMR/MSI-H, IDH1 mutations, FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, BRAF V600E mutations, HER2 overexpression, RET, NTRK1/2/3, or NRG1 fusions.Additional information is available at https://ascopubs.org/guidelines/living-guidelines.

records.title: Multi-institutional study evaluating the role of liquid biopsy to determine risk of extraocular disease, therapy response and recurrence in retinoblastoma.
records.abstract: We analyzed whether changes in RB1 circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) variant allele frequency (VAF) in plasma and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was associated with clinical outcomes in patients with retinoblastoma (RB). We reviewed all RB patients treated at MSKCC and SCEH who had serial plasma and CSF ctDNA analyses. 4/33 intraocular RB patients developed extraocular RB, all associated with an increase in plasma RB1 ctDNA VAF. In the remaining 29 patients who did not develop extraocular disease, RB1 ctDNA remained undetectable. Plasma RB1 ctDNA was positive in 15 of 16 extraocular RB patients at diagnosis and became undetectable in 13 of 14 patients post treatment; the sole patient with rising RB1 ctDNA died of disease. Two stage 4a patients who developed CNS relapse had positive/rising levels of plasma RB1 ctDNA VAF at relapse. 11 patients in remission have undetectable RB1 ctDNA. Two stage 4a patients with residual bony lesions post-chemotherapy but negative ctDNA remain in remission. CSF ctDNA was positive in all 7 patients with central nervous system (CNS) disease at diagnosis and became undetectable post treatment in 3 of 4 patients; the only patient with rising ctDNA died of disease. Two suffered disease recurrence in the CNS post treatment associated with positive/rising levels of CSF RB1 ctDNA VAF. Two stage 4a RB patients had CSF ctDNA positivity at initial diagnosis and recurred in the CNS. Longitudinal ctDNA may predict risk of developing extraocular RB. Its use for monitoring and risk stratification deserves further study.

records.title: Cross-Sectional Profiling of Aqueous Humor VEGF-A Reflects the Tumor and Ocular Microenvironment in Retinoblastoma.
records.abstract: Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) is a key mediator of tumor angiogenesis. This cross-sectional study quantified aqueous humor (AH) VEGF-A in retinoblastoma (RB) eyes and retrospectively evaluated its association with clinical features. This study analyzed 60 AH samples: 54 from 49 RB eyes and 6 from age-matched controls with congenital cataract. From pretreatment RB eyes, six samples were collected prior to globe-salvaging treatment and five immediately after primary enucleation (PE). From post-treatment eyes, 12 samples were collected at secondary enucleation (SE), 12 during active treatment (TX), and 19 at 6 months after treatment (END). VEGF-A was measured using the Olink Proximity Extension Assay and reported as absolute concentrations (pg/mL). VEGF-A concentrations (median and interquartile range [IQR]) were 259 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 140-423, IQR = 115-568) in the RB cohort, compared with 149 (95% CI = 39.8-318, IQR = 61.3-208) in cataract controls. Post-treatment levels were significantly lower than pretreatment levels (median = 182, 95% CI = 121-310, IQR = 110-423 vs. median = 1380, 95% CI = 278-18,100, IQR = 467-12,400, P < 0.001). Among treated eyes, SE samples had higher VEGF-A than END samples (median = 506, 95% CI = 120-1010, IQR = 207-926 vs. median = 129, 95% CI = 79.5-212, IQR = 79.5-212, P = 0.007). AH liquid biopsy was a high-yield source of VEGF-A in RB. VEGF-A concentrations were highest during primary enucleation and normalized after treatment completion. These findings support that aqueous VEGF-A reflects the intraocular microenvironment, warranting further validation to improve our understanding of its role in disease progression in RB.
